::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why is $\tan(\theta)$ the reciprocal of $\tan(90 - \theta)$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2228604/why-is-tan-theta-the-reciprocal-of-tan90-theta), asked by [Toby Mak](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/285313/toby-mak) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-04-11; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Recently, I had a look at [this question on Quora](https://www.quora.com/How-much-is-def-deg-circ-log-tan1-deg+-log-tan2-deg+-log-tan3-deg+-cdots+-log-tan89-deg-when-log-is-a-base-10-logarithm) about how the values of integer tangents from $\tan(1^{\circ})$ to $\tan(90^{\circ})$ sum to $1$. I tried to solve the question on my own here, and got stuck here:
>
> $$\tan(θ) = \frac{1}{\tan(90 - \theta)}$$
>
> $$\tan(θ)\tan(90 - \theta) =  1$$
>
> Please help and, if possible, find more than one solution for this identity (since I know it is commonly used).
:::

Worth remembering: 

> The *cosine* of an angle is the *sine* of its *co*mplement.

I am pretty sure that is why this function is called cosine.  I guess in the days when these values had to be looked up on tables, it was easier to have another column in the table than to add a step to the arithmetic.

The complement of an angle $\theta$ is $90-\theta$.  So
$$\begin{align*}
    \cos(\theta) &= \sin(90-\theta) \\
    \sin(\theta) &= \cos(90-\theta)
\end{align*}$$
Since tangent is sine divided by cosine:
$$\tan(90-\theta) = \frac{\sin(90-\theta)}{\cos(90-\theta)} = \frac{\cos(\theta)}{\sin(\theta)} = \cot(\theta)$$
Again, the *cotangent* of an angle is the *tangent* of its *co*mplement.  Finally, since $\cot(\theta) = \frac{1}{\tan(\theta)}$, your identity is proved.
